blocks.text: Why Chrome is where customer success work happens

Most of a customer success manager's day runs through a browser. Gainsight describes the job as managing many accounts and stakeholders, handling heavy meeting loads, and using email as the main customer channel. The same article lists tracking resolved tickets, churn and upsell opportunities. Each of those lives in a web app, and each web app lives in a Chrome tab.

That is why the browser setup matters. A messy Chrome window makes you hunt for the renewal date before every call. A tidy one gets you there in seconds. The rest of this page covers tab groups, the shortcuts worth memorizing, bookmarks, and the spots where Lazur helps.
How much of the day goes to admin work

The most cited numbers come from Vitally's report, The Secret Lives of CSMs, published in Fall 2023. 66% of CSMs say much of their working day goes to repetitive administrative processes. 63% wish they had more time for client engagement. Admin lives in tabs, so those figures point straight at the browser.

Read these figures with care. Vitally runs the survey itself, and its sample size is not visible in the published page. Treat them as a signal of how CSMs feel about admin, not as a measurement of your team. The pattern still fits the job Gainsight describes: lots of lookups, lots of tabs, and little time to think between them.
Keys to know before you start

Mac shortcuts use a few modifier keys. ⌘ is Command, ⌥ is Option, ⇧ is Shift and ⌃ is Control. Most Chrome shortcuts on a Mac use ⌘. If a guide tells you to press Ctrl, check whether it was written for Windows. Lazur's shortcut is ⌥ and ⌘ held together, so you hold Option and Command to ask it something.
Set up one tab group per customer account

Tab groups are the fastest fix for a crowded window. Put every tab for one account into one group. Then the contract, the support thread, the usage page and the CRM record sit side by side. Collapse the group when you switch accounts, and the rest of the window stays readable.
Chrome's own steps are short. Use this order on your Mac.

items: Right-click a tab, then choose Add tab to group > New group.
Right-click the group's colored circle or name to type the customer's name.
Right-click the same circle or name to pick a color.
Drag other tabs for that account into the group. Dragging also adds tabs to an existing group later.
Click the group name to collapse it. Click it again to expand it.

blocks.text: Name groups after the customer, not the tool. Every account has the same CRM tab and the same mail tab, so tool names repeat. A group called Acme Health tells you where to look when you come back after lunch.
Pick colors with a purpose. You could use red for accounts at risk and green for accounts with an upsell in progress. The colors are your own system. Chrome does not assign any meaning to them.

blocks.title: Keep a Today group
blocks.text: Make one group called Today for open loops. Drop tabs in it during the day. When the day winds down, drag each one back into its account group, or close it.
What tab groups do when Chrome syncs

If browsing history and tabs are synced to your Google Account, group changes save and sync across your devices. That helps when you work on a Mac at the office and on another Mac at home. It also means a mistake travels with the sync.

blocks.title: Deleting spreads to other Macs
blocks.text: Deleting a group, or ungrouping its tabs, also removes the group on other devices that use the same account. Check the other Mac before you clean up.
Chrome shortcuts for account work on Mac
You do not need every Chrome shortcut. You need the ones that move you between accounts and find text fast. The table lists those. Each one is a Mac shortcut from Google's keyboard shortcut page.

blocks.text: Learn ⌘L and ⌘F first. Those two cover most reading and lookup work. Once they feel automatic, add the tab shortcuts. ⌘⌥→ moves you to the next tab in a group, and ⌘1 through ⌘8 jump to a tab by its position.
Find text in long support threads and contracts

Find works on the page you are reading. It does not search your other tabs. Press ⌘F, type the word, and Chrome highlights the matches on the page. Press ⌘G to jump to the next match, and ⌘⇧G to go back.

Here is a worked example. A customer's support thread runs long. They asked about the renewal date twice, and the answer changed. Press ⌘F and type renewal. Press ⌘G until you reach the last mention. Read that message before you reply, because the newest answer is the one that counts.
Mistakes happen when people stop at the first match. Scan the highlighted line and the messages around it. Dates and product names can change between replies, so check the whole exchange.
Bookmark the pages you will need again

Bookmarks help when you return to an account after weeks away. Press ⌘D to bookmark the page you are on. Press ⌘⇧D to save every open tab as a bookmark in a new folder. Press ⌘⌥B to open the Bookmark Manager and tidy up later.

Here is a worked example. Before a quarterly business review, open the contract, the usage page and the support summary. Press ⌘⇧D. Rename the new folder to the customer and the date, so you can find it later. Open that folder from the Bookmark Manager when you need the pages again.

blocks.title: Bookmarks are not your CRM
blocks.text: Keep the official record in your CRM. Use bookmarks for working pages, such as a contract, a dashboard or a shared document. A folder of old links is hard to trust.
Where Lazur fits into your Chrome day

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold Option and Command to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Most of your screen content during a customer day sits in Chrome, so most questions start there.
Point, explain, guide and dictate

items: Point: ask where something is. Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen.
Explain: ask what a page or thread says. Lazur answers out loud from what is on screen.
Guide: ask how to do something. Lazur guides you one click at a time and waits for each click.
Dictate: hold fn and speak. Clean, formatted text lands at the cursor in any app.

blocks.text: Use point when you can see the thing but cannot find it. Use guide when you know the goal but not the steps. Use explain when the text is long and your question is short.

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. When it circles a button, you click it. That is the point of guide mode. You stay in control of every click, and you see what changed.
A worked example: finding a renewal date without hunting
Say you are on a customer's account page, and the renewal date sits in a side panel. The call starts soon. Here is how the exchange goes.

items: Hold Option and Command, then say: where is the renewal date on this page?
Lazur draws a circle and a label around the date, and it says the date out loud.
If the panel is hidden, ask: how do I open the side panel? Lazur guides you one click at a time.
Click the panel yourself. Then compare the date with the signed contract in your bookmarks.

blocks.text: The last step matters most. Lazur reads what is on the screen, and a screen can show an old page. Check the contract whenever a date affects money or a promise to the customer.
Check your Chrome and macOS versions

Version numbers matter for two reasons. Chrome drops older versions of macOS over time. Chrome 151 removes support for macOS 12, and Chrome 150 is the last release that supports it. New Chrome 151 installs need macOS 13 or later.

The current Chrome number is unclear from the sources we checked. Browser Calendar lists Chrome 158.0.8127.18 for Mac, released November 4, 2026. WhatIsMyBrowser lists 156.0.8078.82 for the same date. Open Chrome > About Google Chrome to see the version your copy runs.

items: Chrome version: Chrome > About Google Chrome.
macOS version: Apple menu > About This Mac.
On macOS 12, Chrome 150 is the last release for your Mac, so plan an upgrade with your IT team.

blocks.text: Extensions and the August 31, 2026 cutoff

Some CSM teams run a Chrome extension for a CRM sidebar, a note tool or a sales helper. Google planned to remove all remaining Manifest V2 extensions from the Chrome Web Store by August 31, 2026. That date has passed as of November 7, 2026.

After removal, users and admins cannot update or reinstall those extensions. If a tool you rely on stopped updating, check whether it still appears in the Web Store. Admins should audit extension policies, so ask yours for the current list.

blocks.title: Check your extensions first
blocks.text: List the extensions on your Mac, then note any tool you use every day. Ask your admin whether each one is still supported before your next big account review.
Mistakes that slow down customer success work in Chrome

items: One long row of tabs. Put each account in its own group, and close what you finished.
Grouping by tool. Every group then holds the same CRM and mail tabs, so you lose the account context.
Bookmarking everything. A folder you never open is another search problem.
Using Find as a search across tabs. Find on page checks only the page you are on.
Quoting a number from an old page. Refresh the page before you give a customer a figure.
Deleting a group on one Mac without checking the others. Synced groups vanish on every device.

blocks.text: A short cleanup prevents most of these. Close finished tabs. Move open loops into the Today group. Bookmark the pages you need for tomorrow's first call. Then close the window.
What CSMs say they want automated

The chart uses the same Vitally survey. Admin tasks lead, at 58% of those who want automation. Task organization and prioritization follow at 20%. Client communication is at 13%, and internal communication at 8%.

The admin share suggests where help pays off first. Lookups, copying dates and finding the right message are admin work. A helper that points at things and explains them may save some lookup time. It cannot decide what the customer needs.
Research an account in the background

Before a call with a new stakeholder, you often need recent company news, leadership changes and product launches. Ask Lazur to research the company. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs, not the tabs you have open. It comes back with a summary and a report.
Check the report's sources before you use a fact in an email. A summary is a starting point. Verify any date, figure or name against the source page before it reaches a customer.
Lazur with your email and chat

Much of a CSM's customer contact runs through email and chat. The [Gmail guide](/for/customer-success-managers/gmail) and the [Slack guide](/for/customer-success-managers/slack) cover those tools for customer success work. Lazur helps with the same kinds of questions in each one. Ask it to explain a long thread, or to draft a reply that you check and send yourself.
Set this up this week

items: Create a tab group for each account you handle this week.
Practice ⌘L, ⌘F and ⌘G on one long thread.
Check Chrome > About Google Chrome and Apple menu > About This Mac.
Save the pages for your next big meeting with ⌘⇧D.
Hold Option and Command and ask Lazur where one thing you search for each day sits on screen.

blocks.text: If you want Lazur for these tasks, get the Mac app from the [download page](/download). The trial needs no credit card. Plan details are on the [pricing page](/pricing). For the Chrome side of Lazur, see the [Chrome app page](/apps/chrome).
What this guide could not confirm

We did not find a primary study on how CSMs use browsers. The admin figures come from one vendor survey, and its sample size is not visible. We also could not verify the Gmail template steps, so this guide skips them. The current Chrome version is still disputed between two sources.

faq.question: Do I need Lazur to use these Chrome tips?
faq.answer: No. Tab groups, bookmarks, Find on page and the shortcuts all work in Chrome by themselves. Lazur adds voice help on top. You can skip it and still use everything on this page.

faq.question: Which Chrome shortcuts matter most on a Mac?
faq.answer: Start with ⌘L for the address bar, ⌘F for Find on page and ⌘G for the next match. Add ⌘T and ⌘⇧T when your window fills up. Google's keyboard shortcut page lists the full set.

faq.question: How do I put a tab in a group on a Mac?
faq.answer: Right-click the tab and choose Add tab to group > New group. To add a tab to a group that already exists, drag the tab into the group.

faq.question: Why did a tab group disappear on my other Mac?
faq.answer: Group changes sync when browsing history and tabs are synced to your Google Account. Deleting a group, or ungrouping its tabs, also removes the group on other devices that use the same account.

faq.question: Which Chrome version should I run on a Mac?
faq.answer: Run the latest stable version your Mac supports. Chrome 151 dropped macOS 12, so Chrome 150 is the last release for that version. The sources disagree on the current number, so check Chrome > About Google Chrome.

faq.question: Does Lazur click buttons in Chrome for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points, explains and guides you one click at a time. It does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you.

faq.question: Is my screen recorded when I use Lazur?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: Where do the numbers in this guide come from?
faq.answer: The admin figures come from Vitally's Fall 2023 report, which is a vendor survey with no visible sample size. Shortcut and tab group steps come from Google's Chrome help pages. Treat the survey as a signal, not a measurement.
